name: Cerebras WSE-3 / WSE-3 Turbo (CS-3, CS-4)
memory_bandwidth_basis: CS-3 system page states 44 GB on-chip SRAM and 21 PB/s memory bandwidth for the wafer, i.e. ~21,000 GB/s of on-wafer SRAM bandwidth. IMPORTANT: vram_gb here holds the ON-CHIP SRAM CAPACITY, not VRAM or HBM. The WSE-3 Turbo in CS-4 is quoted at 43.2 PB/s, roughly 2x.

flops.notes: WSE-3 (CS-3 generation), NOT the Turbo. Cerebras CS-3's own spec sheet gives 125 PFLOPS and 21 PB/s for the wafer. Cerebras publishes no precision label and no sparsity statement for this figure, so it is recorded at its face value and flagged dense:true on the basis that Cerebras makes NO sparse claim anywhere for the WSE family - not because Cerebras states it is dense. dense:false here previously asserted a sparsity exemption that Cerebras never published, which is the same class of defect as flagging a correct dense number as non-dense.

WSE-3 TURBO (CS-4 generation, Aug 2026), 3 wafers per system. This is the 250 PFLOPS figure, and it is a DIFFERENT SILICON from the 125,000 row - the Turbo is the faster wafer variant. No precision label is published for it either. Note this is a per-wafer figure quoted by Cerebras and the CS-4 system contains three of them; the 250 PFLOPS is per wafer, not per system, and no system-level total is published.

notes: CORRECTED 2026-10-03 - two defects, both about a claim the vendor never made. (1) The record previously held a single row, fp16 125,000 TFLOPS with dense:false, and its note explained this as 'half of the 250 PFLOPS headline ... the FP16 halving is an assumption, not a vendor statement'. That is the same defect class as the NVIDIA dense-flag bug found elsewhere in this repo, but running in the opposite direction AND it was worse, because the halving was not merely mislabelled - it was fabricated. Cerebras publishes ONE number for the WSE-3 wafer: 125 PFLOPS, on the CS-3 spec sheet, against 21 PB/s. The 250 PFLOPS belongs to the WSE-3 TURBO in CS-4, a different, faster wafer. So 'half of 250' is not a halving at all; it is the CS-3 number coincidentally equal to half the CS-4 number, presented as though Cerebras had published a sparse figure to halve. dense:false also asserted a structured-sparsity exemption that Cerebras has never claimed for any product. Both readings are now separated: 125,000 dense is the CS-3 wafer, 250,000 dense is the CS-3-Turbo wafer, each cited to its own datasheet, and neither is flagged sparse. (2) status was 'verified' at confidence 0.6 while the note simultaneously said the figure's precision was an assumption - a record cannot be verified if the thing being verified is a guess, so it is now contested at 0.55. WHAT IS NOT PUBLISHED, and is therefore left null rather than derived: Cerebras attaches no precision label ('125 PFLOPS of compute'), no sparsity statement, and no dense/sparse split to either figure. 125,000 is therefore recorded under precision 'fp16' purely to satisfy the schema's required enum and is NOT a vendor claim about FP16 - vendor_claim is true only in the sense that Cerebras claims the 125 number. A reader wanting true FP16 tensor throughput on a WSE-3 does not get it from any Cerebras publication. The same applies to memory_bandwidth_basis: 21 PB/s and 43.2 PB/s are Cerebras's own wafer-scale SRAM bandwidth figures and are stated without a methodology. Bandwidth arithmetic: 21,000 GB/s is wafer-scale SRAM bandwidth and reconciles with no bus width because there IS no bus - memory_bus_bit is null and correctly so, since the 44 GB sits on the wafer as distributed SRAM behind the 214 Pb/s on-wafer mesh. vram_gb 44 is ON-CHIP SRAM CAPACITY, not VRAM or HBM, and there is no DRAM tier, so weight streaming from off-package is impossible. That combination - enormous bandwidth, tiny capacity - is only coherent because the working set is resident on the wafer, and it is the structural reason a single wafer cannot hold a 70B model (~140 GB of FP16 weights) and why Cerebras sells multi-wafer systems. THE ROOFLINE CONSEQUENCE worth keeping: ~125-250 PFLOPS against 21-43 PB/s is about 3-6 FLOP/byte, which at batch 1 makes this a bandwidth-bound machine. Scale-out is by adding wafers, and CS-4 puts three Turbo wafers in one system at 2 microseconds wafer-to-wafer latency - that 2 us is the mechanism that keeps decode interactive past 10T parameters. Other figures: 900,000 AI-optimised cores, 4 trillion transistors, 1.2 Tb/s system I/O, 16RU, ~25 kW per node, up to ~USD 3M per node. tdp_w 25000 is the SYSTEM figure for a 16RU node, not a chip TDP, and there is no die-level power figure published. 'Up to 30x faster inference than GPU systems' is vendor benchmarking plus Artificial Analysis and is not a hardware specification. See also asic-cerebras-cs3 and asic-cerebras-cs4.
